documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is expected to revolutionise Australian’s economy with the potential to generate up to $600 billion per annum to GDP by 2030 (Australian Government, Department of Industry, Science and Resources, 2024). To keep up with the accelerating growth of AI, the higher education sector needs to transition from traditional teaching models to an AI-integrated pedagogy. One of the key concerns in this transition is to ensure equitable and sustainable adoption of AI in higher education. This concern is in line with the UNESCO’s recommendation on the ethics of AI (UNESCO,2021). AI adoption in higher education is both complex and consequential, as it may affect educational ethics through economic disparities among students and heterogenous student attitudes towards task fulfillment (Oxfam, 2022; Vacarelu, 2023). Moreover, it is reframing teaching, learning and assessment design, making it increasing difficult to distinguish between authentic effort, mastery, and output (Mills et al., 2025). Undertaken at an Australian university, this research project aims to addresses two pressing questions in contemporary higher education: how students are currently using generative AI (GenAI) for everyday learning tasks, their attitudes towards it and their AI readiness to support transition towards equitable and sustainable engagement with these tools. By revealing these issues, this project ensures student voices are central to ongoing debates about AI in higher education. Hence, this study is both equity-focused and evidenced-based as it responds to a critical gap for evidence-based insights to inform institutional policy development for a more equitable and sustainable digital ecosystem. Best practice suggests that when policies affecting students are designed with their involvement as co-designers, outcomes significantly improve. Therefore, framed as Scholarship of Teaching and Learning (SoTL) research, the project places reflective practice and systematic inquiry at the heart of continuous improvement in teaching and learning outcomes. This study uses a quantitative survey method, whereby a structured questionnaire was administered during semester one, 2026. The questionnaire design is based on the Digital Divide and Self-regulated Learning framework. Data were collected from Humanities students across Law, Accounting, Business, and Education disciplines. Results reveal widespread adoption (98%), with some of it uncritical and potentially over-reliant (similar to Palmer, 2023). Notably, outliers exist where students refuse to use the tools entirely. Overall, findings indicate variation in GenAI usage, attitudes, access, and competence, suggesting the need for targeted interventions to advance equitable and sustainable AI integration. The findings are useful as they inform student-centred teaching practices, curriculum design, and policy frameworks aligned with the university’s commitment to innovative, ethical, and inclusive education.

documents.abstract: Agile project teams promote autonomy, yet little is known about how individuals actually experience autonomy in their day-to-day work. Building on a multiple-case study of five organisations in a manufacturing context with 61 semi-structured interviews, this study analyzes how individuals experience autonomy in agile project work. Drawing on the critical incident technique, complemented by an associative imagery technique, the paper presents a conceptual model of the action area of experienced autonomy, which unfolds through seven interrelated themes: decision-making, owning, realising, information sharing, learning, supporting, and team organising. The analysis of five cases shows how individuals make sense of this action area, revealing autonomy as a relational, contextual, and situational phenomenon. This study contributes to research on autonomy in management research by advancing the understanding of relational autonomy in agile project teams. It highlights autonomy as an experienced action area rather than a static job design feature or motivational characteristic. For managers structuring agile work in production and engineering environments, the findings offer a diagnostic lens to reflect on and support autonomy, fostering a motivating work context. Methodological contribution is achieved by demonstrating the value of associative imagery in capturing abstract and partly tacit aspects of work experience in agile production and engineering contexts.

documents.abstract: The article is devoted to a historical-scientific study of the facts of the biography, personal and human qualities, professional and public activities of Vladimir Markovich Lvov, Doctor of Technical Sciences and Doctor of Psychological Sciences, Professor, a prominent representative of the Tver school of military ergonomics, one of the leaders of the Intersectoral Center for Ergonomic Research and Development Ergocenter (Tver) and the Interregional Ergonomic Association (IEA), and the longstanding Editor-in-Chief of the journal Human Factor: Problems of Psychology and Ergonomics. The article examines the areas and content of his activities aimed at considering the human factor in the development and operation of “human-technology-environment” systems. His leading role in organizing and conducting intersectoral ergonomic research and his fruitful scientific and public activities are noted.

As AI agents take on increasingly open-ended and complex tasks, verifying their outputs has proven to be difficult. Rubric-graded agent environments, where a verifier judges multiple natural-language criteria against the deliverables and environment state changes produced by the agent, have emerged as a popular paradigm. We conduct the first systematic study of verifiers for rubric-graded agent environments. First, we create BankerVerifierBench (BVB), a meta-evaluation dataset of 2,464 human-judged rubric criteria across 24 investment-banking tasks. Next, we develop a methodology that derives from any rubric corpus the capabilities a verifier should possess, yielding a nine-capability taxonomy that we distill into three general design principles---reactive verification, environment alignment, and domain guidance---which we implement in Gandalf, an open-source verifier. Finally, we evaluate Gandalf against three existing verifiers on BVB. Gandalf matches or exceeds every baseline's F1 at lower cost: with Gemini 3 Flash it matches the strongest baseline's F1 (0.864 vs. 0.852) at one-fifth of its cost, and with GPT-5.4 models it improves F1 by over 0.12 at lower cost. Gandalf also generalizes to OpenClaw, a structurally different personal-productivity environment, where it again achieves the highest F1 (0.955 vs. 0.934 for the best baseline). We release BVB, Gandalf, and the code and data to reproduce our experiments.

Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) images have emerged as a promising means for PD recognition. However, constructing a precise DNN-based PD recognition model requires a large number of OCT images and expensive computational resources. This paper aims to transfer pre-trained visual foundation models (VFMs) with the aid of the adapter learning paradigm to recognize PD from OCT images, by adding only a few trainable parameters. We propose a novel VFM-Adapter framework for automatic OCT-based PD recognition based on the adapter learning paradigm. To be specific, we introduce three lightweight adapters: global adapter, local adapter, and token-wise adapter, to effectively leverage the transferability of feature representations from VFMs to OCT images, for equipping VFMs with strong PD recognition capability. Our VFM-Adapter achieves an accuracy of 77.66%, sensitivity of 78.01%, specificity of 77.31%, F1-score of 77.93%, and precision of 79.58%. It outperforms state-of-the-art deep neural networks, such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs), attention-based CNNs, and vision transformers by updating only a small number of parameters. Extensive ablation studies further demonstrated the effectiveness of each adapter. The proposed VFM-Adapter provides an effective yet parameter-efficient transfer learning framework for OCT-based PD recognition. By substantially finetuning the small number of trainable parameters while maintaining competitive PD performance, the proposed framework offers a promising altetnative for automated PD screening in real-world diagnosis scenarios. Not applicable.

Current assurance approaches do not establish whether evidence is sufficient to validate, monitor and govern agentic artificial intelligence (AI) within a pharmaceutical context of use. Plausible outputs may conceal failures in retrieval, reasoning, orchestration or human-control points, where reference standards are unavailable. We developed and operationalised VITAL (Validation by Intended use, Traceability, Autonomy and Lifecycle evidence), a validation framework for agents in clinical development, through landscape analysis, regulatory and standards mapping, expert interviews and multi-stakeholder refinement. VITAL integrates context of use, controls, behavioural validation and lifecycle evidence within a risk-adjusted framework. We applied VITAL across epidemiology and treatment-landscape analysis, site selection, enrolment rescue and trial-design trade-off support to translate autonomy, reversibility, transparency and patient impact into proportionate validation activities, evidence requirements and auditable reconstruction of system behaviour. VITAL may inform evidence requirements and lifecycle accountability for higher-risk pharmaceutical uses; evaluation should assess reproducibility across assessors, organisations and system configurations.

documents.abstract: Video question answering under tight frame budgets requires preserving localized motion and event order, yet current video multimodal large language models (MLLMs) reduce comprehension to static multi-image reasoning by discarding unselected frames and encoding keyframes independently: (1) Spatially, whole-frame pooling dilutes small moving targets into static backgrounds; (2) Temporally, dropping intermediate frames or averaging tokens erases inter-frame motion, confusing direction, speed, and order. We propose VIVID (Visual Inter-frame Variations and Individual Dynamics), which moves beyond static snapshots like human vision: keyframes capture core states while inter-frame Patch Diffs preserve neighboring changes within $K_f$ keyframes. Autonomous Delta-Driven Keyframe Planning (ADKP) selects anchors from a $3\text{ fps}$ pool and feeds surrounding patch differences into Dual-Road Change Memory (DRCM), forming Dynamic Tokens at zero extra anchor tokens alongside a camera-stabilized Active Motion Region of Interest (ROI) and chronological Entity State Chains. Adding $0.22\%$ trainable parameters to a frozen $27\text{B}$ backbone, VIVID-Small ($50$ examples, $\sim 1.5$ GPU hours) beats all eleven baselines in overall accuracy across $8,083$ questions and trails only VIVID-Large ($3,600$ examples), which leads on MotionBench, Video-MME, and TempCompass.

documents.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on text, but whether pretrained LLMs are effective for large-scale tabular classification remains unclear, as many previous works demonstrate that LLMs' tabular data classification performance falls behind tree-based models or neural architectures designed for tabular data. At Visa Research, we managed to fine-tune a pretrained Llama 3.2 1B LLM on billions of rows of labeled tabular data and make it outperform a wide array of tabular classifiers and even our competitive production deep learning model. For ease of reference, we refer to the model as the Visa Research LLM (VRLLM). In this paper, we share how we achieved this exciting result, covering data preparation, training recipe, ablation studies of design choices and deployment validation. We also benchmark frontier LLMs on the same task and analyze their prediction behavior across model families and generations. Our interpretability experiments suggest that VRLLM learns feature-specific predictive associations, while component ablations indicate that the earliest two FFN layers contribute to the emergence of linearly decodable task information. Our paper provides an engineering recipe and a focused empirical case study on adapting compact LLMs to industrial tabular prediction tasks.

Reward design remains a central bottleneck in reinforcement learning (RL), particularly in sparse-reward, long-horizon and partially observable settings requiring dependency chaining, memory, and deceptive affordance disambiguation. While recent foundation-model approaches reduce manual reward engineering, most assume goal-conditioning, task descriptions, expert demonstrations, or ground-truth metrics. These assumptions are problematic in partially observable environments, where task-relevant objectives, affordances, and dynamics must be discovered through interaction rather than disclosed a priori. We formalise this problem setting by introducing WATERFALL, an iterative population-based workflow for automated reward discovery under the strict observability constraints inherent in POMDP environments. WATERFALL achieves this by (i) synthesising diverse programmatic reward candidates via persona-conditioned generation, (ii) evaluating candidate behaviour from raw visual rollouts utilising a Swiss-system evolutionary tournament judged by vision-language models to identify elites, and (iii) leveraging longitudinal assessment histories to iteratively mutate, escalate, or prune candidates. We evaluate WATERFALL across fully observable and reveal-gated partially observable environments ranging from discrete to continuous, comparing against sparse-reward RL, intrinsic-motivation and foundation-model reward-synthesis baselines. Our results indicate that WATERFALL discovers and refines reward programs without access to privileged information, outperforming baselines that retain their native information advantages, most clearly in the POMDP regime. Extensive ablations substantiate that visual evidence, tournament-based selection, and iterative refinement are jointly important. Enforcing this contract is what separates autonomous reward discovery from benchmark-privileged reward shaping.

Crypto-asset service providers increasingly meet users through websites, wallet-connect flows, and other public interfaces, but the legal duties attached to that visible layer remain fragmented across licensing, AML/CFT, marketing, consumer-protection, privacy, tax, and stablecoin regimes. Existing comparative accounts usually map regulatory perimeter and licensing architecture rather than the user-visible disclosure layer. This article maps de jure obligations and legally relevant compliance signals at the public interfaces of crypto-asset service providers across twenty-two jurisdictional units, using FATF standards and selected international policy materials as reference points. It develops a 15-category matrix that separates binding duties, conditional legal duties, inferred supervisory signals, prudential signals, and areas where no website-facing requirement was identified. The article treats the website as a regulatory disclosure interface and offers a structured starting point for jurisdiction-specific legal analysis, regulator-facing guidance, and future empirical audits of actual website compliance. A separately stated normative proposal connects consumer choice and entrepreneurial freedom to a country-of-origin regime for functionally integrated online services, with responsibility allocated across human–machine systems and agent-mediated interactions. This proposal is distinguished from the legal mapping and is not presented as an existing international exemption.

This practice-based and philosophical paper reflects on human collaboration with AI agents, especially for learning expert-level skills in higher education. Using the development of the AI-supported multi-agent system LASSI as an example, it narrates a learning journey in three phases: productive amazement, a shift in authorship, and finally taking responsibility. Perspectives of a developer, a professor, and students show how human-agent systems change through collaboration. Three philosophical dimensions – embodied knowledge, enhanced technologies, and embedded ethics – are used to assess potentials and risks: what happens when intelligence is disembodied, human capabilities are outsourced to technology, and values are encoded? The paper argues that agents should not be treated as neutral tools but as co-shapers within the sociotechnical system of education. It concludes by portraying universities as thinking workshops that must redefine their role with AI: away from exam-driven routines toward cultivating judgment and self-reflection.

documents.abstract: Higher education has responded to generative AI largely by regulating it by task, specifying where the technology may or may not be used in each assessment. This paper argues that task-based regulation uses the wrong unit of analysis. A single task typically spans several types of cognitive work, and a tool that can be welcomed for one type may quietly displace another. This conceptual paper proposes a four-level framework of cognitive engagement, adapted from classical Chinese expressions about knowing and articulated in contemporary cognitive terms: broad knowledge acquisition, analogical transfer, contextual inference, and original creation. The levels are ordered along a single axis, from cognitive work that is codifiable and reducible to rules and patterns, to work that is situated and dependent on human judgement. This axis maps closely onto the boundary of what generative AI can and cannot do: capability is near-complete at the codifiable end and degrades sharply as work becomes situated. The framework thus functions as a diagnostic lens for design, allowing educators to assign AI a role matched to the cognitive work a task is meant to develop. Two illustrative cases show the framework guiding differentiated, defensible decisions about AI integration within a single assessment.

documents.abstract: An agent resource's value depends on its backbone and companion resources and is known only after execution. Token-based generators remain tied to their training catalog, while independent resource scoring misses complementarities and reused bundles target other tasks. We formulate Task-Conditioned Agent Resource Composition (AgentComposition): jointly selecting a backbone model and a tool-skill bundle to maximize end-to-end execution utility. Our Retrieval-Grounded Bundle-Aware Agent Generation retrieves candidate resources and past configurations of similar tasks. A fine-tuned generator reads resource descriptions and recombines candidates through constrained beam search, allowing new resources without retraining. A bundle-aware critic ranks complete configurations using a large language model (LLM) teacher and historically successful configurations as execution proxies, and adapts to execution feedback when available. We evaluate reference recovery, offline execution with judged and native rewards, and online recommendation with real execution, building AgentSelect-Exec with 5,060 executed configurations. Our method recovers the complete reference configuration within ten candidates for 67.73% of AgentSelect queries, nearly twice the strongest baseline, and leads all baselines on SkillsBench. The proxy-trained critic raises the top-ranked agent's execution score from 7.58 to 8.37 out of 10; execution feedback increases it to 8.78, above the strongest baselines. Four target-domain queries suffice to adapt the generator to SkillsBench. Agents recommended online outperform the strongest baselines under both an LLM judge and native verifiers. These results support learning and transferring joint resource composition from task experience.

Universities govern AI adoption through artefacts. Policies, rubrics, assessment briefs, vendor evaluation frameworks, and design templates cross organisational boundaries and carry meaning differently in each context. This paper applies the concept of boundary objects within a cultural-historical activity theory (CHAT) framework to analyse which artefacts effectively mediate AI governance across academic, institutional, and commercial activity systems, and which fail. Drawing on the author’s framework for negotiated legitimacy in interacting activity systems and reflexive practitioner experience as an education design leader, the paper develops a typology of AI governance boundary objects classified by origin, interpretive flexibility, and failure mode. The analysis identifies three structural conditions that determine whether a boundary object supports or undermines the legitimacy of learning designers who broker AI adoption across systems. These are co-design across activity systems, support for transformation rather than coordination alone, and resistance to capture by a single system’s logic. It also identifies a failure dynamic specific to generative AI, in which an unstable referent causes artefacts to decay. The paper offers practical design principles for governance artefacts and connects them to a wider question, namely how institutions keep human and pedagogical judgement central as they adopt digital technologies.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in higher education, yet much of its use positions AI as a private productivity tool for generating answers, feedback or text. This paper argues that AI is not educational simply because it produces outputs. From a sociocultural perspective, its educational significance emerges when pedagogical design transforms it from an artefact into a mediating tool for participation in disciplinary learning. The paper introduces the AI Mediated Participation Framework, grounded in mediated learning, appropriation and participation. It proposes three design principles: preserving learner ownership, scaffolding thinking through dialogue, and developing AI literacy through disciplinary practice. These principles operate through questioning, dialogue, reflection, critical evaluation and decision making to support learner agency, evaluative judgement, responsible AI use, critical thinking and knowledge construction. The framework is illustrated through AI learning activities in undergraduate and postgraduate educational research courses, where educator modelling, peer discussion and disciplinary expectations repositioned AI from a private feedback service to a mediating tool for methodological reasoning and researcher judgement. The framework shifts attention from what AI can do to how pedagogical design determines what AI becomes educationally.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly entering knowledge work, and its short-term productivity benefits are increasingly documented. Less is known about what happens, over time, to the knowledge, skills, and judgment that remain in people and organizations. This integrative narrative review addresses that question through the construct of cognitive capital: the accumulated, renewable, and depletable stock of knowledge, cognitive, and metacognitive capabilities, and practices that enable an individual or an organization to learn, interpret information, exercise judgment, solve problems, and adapt. We distinguish individual and organizational cognitive capital from the capability of the human-AI system, so that gains in joint performance and losses in human capability can be observed at the same time. Drawing on experimental, field, and conceptual work, we propose four mechanisms through which interaction with AI affects cognitive capital: substitution of practice, scaffolding and feedback, metacognitive calibration, and organizational aggregation. Seven principles summarize the current evidence, including that assisted performance differs from retained competence, that the same technology can support or displace learning depending on design and use, and that individual gains can coexist with reduced collective diversity. For each mechanism, we derive testable propositions, and we discuss five design levers for organizations as proposals to be validated rather than established practice. We conclude that cognitive capital offers a multilevel frame for governing AI adoption and outline a research agenda centered on longitudinal, multilevel measurement.

Educators are increasingly turning to generative AI when developing teaching materials, yet most research to date has centred on student-facing applications. This paper presents a work-in-progress study that asks a different question: what happens to an educator’s design judgment when AI enters the case-writing process? Two business educators – one in accounting, one in management – will each develop a teaching case study using AI-assisted workflows, documenting their prompts, editorial decisions, and reasoning through structured process logs. Drawing on Schön’s (1983) reflective practitioner framework and Abell’s (1997) 10 criteria for effective teaching cases, the study examines where human expertise proves essential and where AI contributes meaningfully. The pairing of two sub-disciplines, management accounting and management, allows us to examine whether disciplinary knowledge shapes these design decisions in distinct ways, although the study’s central concern remain the design judgement itself. Early observations from the instrument development phase point to a useful distinction: AI appears better suited to qualities that require evaluative judgment (structure, data accuracy, length) than those demanding generative judgment (ambiguity, controversy, authentic voice). We expect further patterns to emerge once data collection begins. This paper outlines the research design and its anticipated contributions.

Purpose Novice university teachers often start without any formal preparation or education in teaching. This means that they develop their competencies through hands-on teaching experiences. These new and unfamiliar experiences can create tensions. Previous research suggests that tensions may provide opportunities for professional growth, but offers little understanding of how this learning process unfolds. Building on theories of workplace learning, this study aims to explore when and how novice university teachers’ tensions may lead to learning by identifying key antecedents, learning activities and learning mechanisms. Design/methodology/approach A longitudinal multiple case study was conducted including eight junior lecturers. Data were collected via weekly diaries and semi-structured interviews at the beginning and end of the academic year 2023-2024, and analyzed using thematic analysis. Findings The results show that novice university teachers learning from tension depends on a complex interplay between tension characteristics (e.g. intensity), individual antecedents (e.g. perfectionism, self-doubt) and contextual antecedents (e.g. social support). Together, these antecedents enabled or inhibited engagement in learning activities (e.g. collegial conversations), which ultimately fostered diverse learning outcomes through mechanisms such as perspective-taking or social validation. Practical implications The findings provide guidance for higher education policymakers and developers of professional development programs on how to foster supportive learning environments for novice university teachers. Originality/value This study offers in-depth insights into when and how novice university teachers learn from workplace tensions. By linking general theories of workplace learning to the study of tensions, it sheds light on the antecedents, activities and mechanisms that contribute to novice university teachers’ learning from tensions.

This non-empirical conceptual analysis examines how artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming woven into curriculum production, assessment, feedback, student support, academic integrity, accessibility and institutional decision-making. These systems are often justified through connection: faster feedback, personalised support, scalable services and more efficient learning design. Yet technical connection is not the same as educational connection. AI may leave the visible forms of university learning intact while weakening academic authorship, assessment validity, student trust, staff agency, care, equity and institutional legitimacy. The paper develops refusal-capable design: the distributed institutional capacity to decide when AI should be adopted, constrained, redesigned or refused. It integrates connected learning, responsible innovation, sociotechnical studies of educational technology, care ethics, justice-oriented educational judgment and technology non-use scholarship, using selected public examples illustratively rather than as an empirical sample. Six heuristic refusal zones organise recurring legitimacy tensions, and the Distributed Refusal-Capable University Design Cycle translates those tensions into accountable redesign. The contribution is a practical and theoretical account of refusal as a legitimate design outcome rather than simple opposition to AI.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Typed decision models combine natural-language understanding with a structured interface that returns a selected action and an option-level probability distribution without generating lengthy textual responses. Their low inference cost and response latency make them attractive for transportation problems with predefined alternatives. This paper investigates their effectiveness, robustness, and efficiency in two representative transportation tasks: individual travel-mode choice prediction and sequential traffic signal control. We systematically evaluate TypeSafe Jev and GPT-6 Luna Decisions against conventional transportation methods, reinforcement learning algorithms, and four chat-based large language models. Experiments on the Swissmetro dataset show that typed decision models achieve lower prediction accuracy than traditional discrete choice models and the strongest chat-based baseline, while their performance varies substantially with input representation and question framing. In closed-loop traffic signal control experiments, typed decision models demonstrate competitive performance against established controllers in several scenarios, but exhibit performance degradation under more challenging network conditions. Furthermore, the typed models achieve lower inference latency and computational cost than the evaluated chat-based large language models, highlighting their potential for efficient, zero-shot transportation decision-making. Overall, these findings demonstrate both the potential and limitations of typed decision models, emphasizing the importance of input design, task characteristics, and robustness evaluation for their effective application in transportation systems.

Human-centred learning design requires more than using generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) to make assessment feedback faster, more accessible or scalable. It requires attention to whether human judgement, relationships and responsibility remain visible when feedback is produced. The public is a key stakeholder in these decisions because university qualifications operate as public credentials whose legitimacy depends on confidence in how achievement is judged and certified. Yet debate has largely focused on students’ use of GenAI, with less attention given to public expectations of academic practice when GenAI contributes to feedback. This exploratory study surveyed 299 participants, most of whom had current or previous experience of higher education, to examine the implied obligations underpinning university assessment and feedback. Participants strongly endorsed feedback as an expected component of university teaching and generally supported disclosure of GenAI use, meaningful academic involvement and visible instructor responsibility. Exploratory factor analysis identified two provisional dimensions: AI feedback transparency and legitimacy, and assessment expectations and feedback value, although the second demonstrated only modest internal consistency. Interpreted through psychological contract theory, the findings suggest that human-centred GenAI implementation depends not only on feedback quality or efficiency but also on preserving visible academic judgement, accountability and educational purpose. The central design distinction is therefore between GenAI that supports academic practice and GenAI that substitutes for meaningful academic engagement.

The rapid integration of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) into educational settings has been increasingly framed as a transformative opportunity for learning, especially in relation to Social-Emotional Learning (SEL) and Intercultural Competence (IC). Generative AI systems and adaptive learning platforms, including conversational interfaces and adaptive feedback mechanisms, are increasingly positioned as tools for mediating educational interactions (Riordan Alfredo et al., 2024;Holmes & Tuomi, 2022). However, this assumption obscures a critical issue. Research on Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIED) highlights that educational AI encompasses diverse technological applications and involves not only technological design but also questions concerning adoption, impacts, challenges, and the ways in which such systems shape teaching and learning processes (Wang et al., 2024). From a critical perspective, generative AI systems and adaptive learning platforms can therefore be understood not as neutral tools, but as sociotechnical infrastructures that may reflect and reproduce certain epistemological, cultural, and political assumptions about what counts as information, knowledge, communication, appropriate social interaction, and educational practice (Williamson & Eynon, 2020).In this sense, AI-mediated education refers not simply to the use of educational systems, particularly generative and adaptive learning systems, in classrooms, but to the reconfiguration of educational relationships through algorithmic systems that intervene between teachers, learners, knowledge, and peers (Kuhail et al., 2023). The convergence of generative AI systems and adaptive learning platforms may increasingly shape educational processes through prediction, optimisation, and algorithmic mediation (Turvey & Pachler, 2026;Riordan Alfredo et al., 2024). Instead of direct human-to-human interaction, educational processes increasingly take the form of mediated exchanges, such as student-AI-teacher or student-AI-student interactions, enabled particularly by generative AI systems and adaptive learning systems, where algorithms may shape, filter, or mediate elements of dialogue, collaboration, feedback, and critical thinking (Bayne, 2024;Williamson et al., 2020).It is important to note that AI-mediated education does not refer to a homogeneous category of technologies. Contemporary educational AI includes generative AI systems (i.e., large language model-based tutors and conversational agents), adaptive learning platforms, automated assessment tools, machine translation technologies, and other data-driven educational systems that operate through different technical architectures and pedagogical logics (Riordan Alfredo et al., 2024;Holmes et al., 2019). Recent scholarship has highlighted substantial variation in the degree of human control, automation, stakeholder involvement, and educational mediation across systems (Riordan Alfredo et al., 2024). The present opinion paper focuses primarily on generative AI systems and adaptive learning environments, because these technologies can increasingly mediate educational interactions, shape learning pathways, and influence how learners may encounter knowledge, feedback, and social relations. Consequently, the arguments outlined here should not be interpreted as applying equally to all forms of educational AI. While some applications, such as machine translation and accessibility tools, may facilitate communication and participation without fundamentally restructuring educational relationships, generative AI systems and adaptive learning systems may raise more substantial questions regarding algorithmic mediation, epistemic authority, and the democratic purposes of education. Accordingly, the potential consequences discussed in the following sections are considered primarily in relation to generative AI systems and adaptive learning environments, rather than being generalised across all educational AI technologies.This transformation is particularly significant for domains such as SEL and IC, both of which depend on exposure to difference, relational engagement, and negotiation of meaning (Deardorff, 2006;Cipriano & McCarthy, 2023). SEL in this opinion paper is understood in its main formulation as a framework for developing various competencies, such as self-awareness and social awareness, self-management, and relationship skills (CASEL, 2021). However, SEL is not just a set of individual competencies, but a socially, culturally, and relationally embedded process, through which learners understand emotions, norms, and relationships, negotiate social meanings, encounter different perspectives, and develop the capacity to engage constructively with disagreement. From this perspective, SEL depends not only on emotional regulation but also on participation in shared spaces of dialogue and collective meaning. SEL is consequently a situated process that intersects with power, identity and communication within educational contexts.The connection between SEL and IC can be understood more explicitly through their shared relational and dialogical foundations. In Deardorff's (2006) conceptualisation, intercultural competence is not limited to the acquisition of knowledge about cultural groups but involves attitudes, skills, and dispositions that are developed through engagement with cultural difference, including openness, respect, perspective-taking, and the ability to negotiate meaning. Similarly, contemporary approaches to SEL emphasise that social-emotional capacities develop through relationships, communication, perspective-taking, and the interpretation of social situations rather than through isolated individual skill acquisition (CASEL, 2021;Cipriano & McCarthy, 2023). From a relational and dialogical perspective, these processes necessarily involve encounters with perspectives that are not fully predictable or identical to one's own. Ambiguity and disagreement therefore constitute not merely potential difficulties but important conditions for developing interpretive flexibility, perspective-taking, and the capacity to negotiate meaning. Democratic educational theory further extends this relational logic by positioning plurality, dialogue, and constructive disagreement as conditions of participation in a shared world (Biesta, 2022;Dewey, 1916Dewey, /2018;;Freire, 1970Freire, /2005)). Taken together, these perspectives suggest that SEL and IC share a common relational foundation: both are developed through encounters with others, negotiation of meaning, engagement with difference, and the capacity to remain open to perspectives that cannot be fully predetermined. Democratic schooling provides the broader collective context in which these capacities can be enacted, tested, and developed through participation and dialogue.From this perspective, SEL is sustained not only through emotional regulation but through ambiguity, co-construction, dialogue, and the negotiation of disagreement⎯conditions that may sit uneasily with high predictive and optimisation-oriented forms of algorithmic mediation (Mesquita et al., 2026). Empirical research on generative AI and AI-supported translation tools suggests that these technologies may support intercultural learning by facilitating communication, translation, and access to multiple perspectives (Akhrenova & Moradkhani, 2026). However, this form of mediation also raises theoretical and normative concerns about standardisation, cultural bias, and the possibility that AI may mediate rather than simply facilitate intercultural encounters (Ali et al., 2024;Holmes et al., 2019). Consequently, it also raises critical questions about the nature of social interaction, the role of disagreement, and the conditions under which intercultural and democratic learning take place (Andreotti, 2021;CoE, 2018).Therefore, this opinion paper aims to critically examine how AI-mediated educational settings reconfigure social interaction and to explore the conditions under which such mediation may either strengthen or constrain IC, SEL, and democratic schooling. Rather than treating generative AI and adaptive learning systems as inherently harmful or beneficial, the paper focuses on the pedagogical and relational conditions under which AI-mediated interaction may expand participation, access, and opportunities for dialogue, while also potentially reshaping the conditions of interpersonal and democratic engagement.Towards this endeavour, we first argue that AI-mediated education is not a neutral enhancement of learning, but a form of algorithmic mediation that may shape how learners encounter knowledge, others, and difference (Turvey & Pachler, 2026). Second, we argue that although AI may enhance accessibility and communication, it may also potentially reduce some forms of ambiguity, unpredictability, and productive tension that are theoretically important to both intercultural and social-emotional learning (Turvey & Pachler, 2026). Third, we argue that generative AI systems and adaptive learning systems may contribute to the individualisation of learning and the optimisation of interaction, potentially constraining collective meaning-making processes that are essential to democratic education (Biesta, 2022;Selwyn, 2019). Finally, we argue that generative AI and adaptive learning systems should be understood as supplementary technologies within democratically governed educational frameworks rather than as substitutes for human relationality and dialogical engagement (Wieczorek, 2025;Jin & Wang, 2025). This aligns with calls for democratically governed approaches to educational AI that foreground collective oversight, ethical accountability, and participatory design in the development and deployment of AI systems in education (Kerssens & van Es, 2025).The theoretical contribution of this opinion paper lies not in introducing algorithmic sociality as a new concept, but in extending its analytical relevance to educational interaction. We argue that algorithmic sociality helps explain a dimension that is less directly captured by accounts of algorithmic governance, datafication, platformisation, or technological mediation: how changes in the mode of mediation can reconfigure the relational conditions of educational encounter. Drawing on broader scholarship on algorithmic sociality and governance, we theoretically infer that, in AImediated education, prediction, personalisation, filtering, and automated feedback may do more than redistribute knowledge or organise learning processes; they may reshape learners' opportunities to encounter ambiguity, negotiate difference, engage with disagreement, and participate in collective meaning-making. documents.abstract: Abstract Students increasingly practise with multiple-choice questions (MCQs) generated by large language models (LLMs). However, an MCQ-based assessment can reliably measure knowledge only when the correct answer is equally likely to occur in every answer position. A recent preprint demonstrated that LLMs exhibit non-uniform answer-position distributions under deterministic decoding. This study investigates a narrower and empirically testable question: whether answer-position bias generalises across model families and versions beyond those examined previously, whether it persists under sampling and prompting conditions representative of routine usage, and whether it can be mitigated through explicit instructions to balance answer keys. We generated 2,819 MCQs, including 2,109 produced using a standard prompt, with gemini-3-flash-preview, gpt-oss-120b, and qwen3.8-27b. The experimental variables included temperature (0–1), batch size (5–25 questions per request), number of answer options (four or five), and prompt wording. Statistical analyses treated the 293 generation requests, rather than individual questions, as the independent experimental units. All three models systematically under-utilised the final answer position, with a pooled empirical frequency of 6.1% (128/2,109), substantially below the expected uniform probability of 20–25%. The preferred answer position remained relatively stable across versions within model families (B for Qwen and B/C for Gemini), whereas the newly examined gpt-oss family exhibited a distinct preference for position A. Variations in temperature, batch size, option count, and prompt wording did not eliminate this bias. An explicit one-sentence instruction to balance answer positions substantially mitigated the bias in two models but was ineffective for Qwen. Moreover, for gpt-oss, this intervention introduced incorrectly keyed questions, affecting 7.2% of the generated items. We further demonstrate the practical implications of this systematic bias: a position-based guessing strategy, calibrated using independent generation requests, correctly predicts 38–57% of previously unseen answers, compared with the nominal chance-level performance of 25%. Finally, we explicitly distinguish the findings that extend previous observations, those that independently reproduce earlier results, and those that qualify existing conclusions. These results highlight the need for systematic answer-key validation and position-bias auditing when LLM-generated MCQs are used for educational assessment.

This conceptual position paper reframes knowledge sharing as informal peer learning in digitally mediated professional environments. It addresses a gap in existing knowledge-sharing and socio-technical explanations which do not sufficiently explain how social conditions interact with digital mechanisms to shape both contribution and recognition. Using theory adaptation and model development, the paper integrates cultural context, generational identity, relational conditions, self-determined motivation, and a cross-cutting socio-digital mediation environment. The model distinguishes willingness to share, opportunity to participate, and the subsequent visibility and recognition of contributions. Its propositions explain how psychological safety mediates contextual influences, how opportunity, power, and risk condition motivation, and how platform affordances and algorithmic visibility shape participation and recognition. The contribution is a human-centred framework for analysing who contributes, who remains silent, and whose knowledge becomes visible and valued, while informing more inclusive workplace learning, professional learning networks, and digitally mediated communities of practice.

Background Generative AI (GenAI) can now produce artefacts such as essays, literature reviews, and worked rationales which challenge assessment designs that reward the products of thinking over the practice of it (Bearman et al., 2024; Corbin et al., 2025; Dawson et al., 2024). In evidence-based practice (EBP) education, students are required to appraise study quality, interpret effect sizes, and integrate findings into clinical decisions (Lehane et al., 2019). GenAI can now generate convincing outputs for each of these tasks. Observational data on what students do cognitively when they use GenAI in EBP tasks are scarce. Depending on how students use it, GenAI may scaffold the reasoning that EBP education is designed to develop or may bypass it (Vendrell & Johnston, 2026). Aim This study explores how allied health students engage with GenAI, how much they rely on it, and how they reason about its use when completing an EBP evidence-appraisal task. Methods This is an exploratory qualitative study using a concurrent think-aloud protocol with allied health students who have completed an EBP unit. The unit must have included critical reasoning as a learning outcome. Participants complete a structured 60-minute EBP task involving a clinical scenario. During this task, participants verbalise their reasoning and rationale for using or declining GenAI. A researcher facilitates this process through non-directive questions. Sessions are audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analysed in two stages. In the first stage, transcripts are coded deductively and inductively against the six critical thinking processes in Vendrell and Johnston’s (2026) framework: conceptual interpretation, inferential reasoning, evaluative judgement, metacognitive regulation, intellectual curiosity, and epistemic integrity. This stage identifies whether and how reasoning is handed over to GenAI. In the second stage, an interpretive analysis informed by critical pedagogy (Freire, 2005) examines how students position themselves in relation to AI-generated knowledge. Freire described a banking model of education, in which an authority deposits knowledge into passive students. This model offers a lens for examining uncritical acceptance of GenAI output, should that be present (Freire, 2005). Freire located authority in the school system and in the teacher who deposits knowledge into students (Freire, 2005). GenAI is a further candidate for that position in higher education. Unlike a teacher or an institution, it is designed by companies whose incentive is engagement and commercial return rather than student learning (Bartsch et al., 2025). Findings Data collection is in progress. This study will generate think-aloud data on how allied health students engage cognitively with GenAI during EBP appraisal tasks, mapping where GenAI use aligns with or diverges from the reasoning processes EBP education is designed to develop. The interpretive analysis will explore the degrees of agency students exercise over AI-generated knowledge and the conditions in which they exercise or relinquish it, which process-level coding alone cannot capture. Conclusion Findings may inform teaching and assessment design in EBP units and provide a think-aloud protocol that can be adapted to examine GenAI use in reasoning tasks across health professions education.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often described in terms of personas and this framing has become central to alignment research. In this paper, we argue that there is a deeper level of description that lies in the agent's worldviews, i.e., its beliefs about what reality is and how it works. Treating LLMs as a population of subjects, we administer two worldview surveys from human psychology to eight models. We show that the models share many key worldview positions. For example, LLMs consistently describe the world as less good, safe, enticing, and alive than humans do. On the other hand, base models have a more positive outlook, suggesting that the bleakness we found is driven by post-training. In line with research on LLM "personas", we show that system prompts eliciting different identities shift worldviews in consistent directions, and that a contemplative prompt creates a more positive outlook and improves safety. We also found that dialogue between models consistently shifts worldviews and that several models converge on the "spiritual bliss" attractor. Intriguingly, dialogue increased safe responses and the spiritual bliss attractor engendered the most aligned responses overall. These findings suggest that worldviews form a measurable and malleable layer of LLM behavior that may be crucial for robust, positive alignment.

documents.abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence can reproduce many instructional and social behaviors of human tutors, but students may interpret those behaviors differently depending on who they believe is providing them. We examined how perceived tutor identity shapes students' evaluations of instructional feedback, satisfaction of psychological needs according to Self-Determination Theory, and their communication strategies with tutors. In a within-subjects Wizard-of-Oz study, 27 introductory computer science students completed two text-based tutoring sessions involving Python code-explanation problems. Participants were told one tutor was human and the other was AI, although the same human provided feedback in both conditions. We found participants evaluated both tutors favorably and reported few consistent differences in the instructional value of the feedback. However, participants frequently questioned whether AI could genuinely care about them, which corresponded with the human tutor having higher scores of relatedness need satisfaction. Human presence offered connection and accountability for some participants but introduced anxiety in others. Participants also reported communicating more casually with the human tutor and more explicitly with the AI tutor. These findings suggest complementary roles for human and AI tutoring and highlight the importance of considering psychological needs alongside instructional quality.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used for emotional and mental health support (EMS), a process in which users often described GenAI as empathic and friend-like. These descriptions suggest that people may develop imaginations of GenAI chatbots that may reflect their interpersonal needs and desires. The objective of this study is to systematically explore and thematically organizethe imaginations of GenAI among users who repeatedly use GenAI for EMS. In April 2024, we recruited 270 adults from 29 countries who had repeatedly utilized GenAI for EMS. Participants provided qualitative data regarding their imagination of ChatGPT. The analysis followed a structured reflexive thematic analysis approach. We identified two meta- themes: a) Entity (the “what”), which described the kind of beings or things they imagine GenAI as, appearing in 86.3% ( n = 233) of responses, and b) Trait (the "how"), which described users’ descriptions of perceived capacities of these beings, appearing in 36% (n = 96) of responses. The “Entity” descriptions clustered along two dimensions : abstract–concrete and human–nonhuman, which intersect to form a four-quadrant conceptual space containing 11 subthemes ranging from unbounded energy and spiritual beings to humans and robots . The “Traits” meta-theme fell into five themes: physical traits and manifestations (“looking”), cognitive abilities (“knowing”), productivity (“doing”), emotional abilities (“feeling”), and rapport (“relating”). The findings provide a systematic categorization of imaginations of GenAI for EMS, showing that GenAI is not only used as an informational tool but also imagined sometimes as an all-knowing, powerful, and highly interpersonal being. These imaginations can be highly relevant for examining human–AI relationships and underscore the need to examine how such imaginations relate to benefits and risks of AI chatbot use for mental health.
