topics: Numerical Solvers for Ordinary Differential Equations

documents.abstract: It is commonly understood that factoring a general $n$-bit biprime via Shor's order finding algorithm requires $\widetilde{O}(n^3)$ gates by leveraging schoolbook integer arithmetics for addition and multiplication. Recent developments in quantum arithmetic circuits leveraging recursive Toom-Cook schemes have improved the cost scaling to $O(n^{2+ε})$. Here $ε>0$ depends on algorithm implementation details of the recursive multiplication steps, which allow for a vast number of design choices. The challenge in navigating such design space also presents an opportunity for demonstrating innovative practices in quantum software engineering in the era of open agentic science. We present a formally verified harness that ingests a design specification (namely a "policy" that describes a recursive circuit design scheme) from an external source, which may be an AI agent, and produces a set of formalized proofs covering mathematical correctness of the algorithm implementation, asymptotic scaling of the end-to-end gate cost, as well as the correctness of translating the verified algorithm to a detailed circuit implementation with an intermediate representation. The harness is published as an open challenge where human researchers and AI agents can search for more efficient factoring circuits while retaining machine-checked guarantees of correctness and end-to-end asymptotic complexity.

Artificial intelligence regulation has become a central concern for scholars and policymakers. This article argues that AI-centered regulatory frameworks will become increasingly inadequate as automation becomes ubiquitous and embedded in social institutions. Drawing on risk society, sociotechnical systems, and adaptive governance theory, it proposes an expected shift toward activity-based governance supported by a layered regulatory architecture capable of remaining effective under conditions of technological uncertainty and conceptual instability.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can make decisions that affect other agents, but what happens after a harmful or unsuccessful interaction remains poorly understood. We investigate whether apologies by LLM agents are associated with subsequent cooperative behaviour, using controlled Prisoner's Dilemma experiments with four commercial models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and Mistral Large 3). Across payoff conditions, we examine when agents apologise, the reasons they provide, and the actions that follow. We also examine how access to one round of interaction history affects behaviour and, in a second experiment, whether and how agents offer compensation alongside their apologies. Apology behaviour differed substantially across models and preceding interaction outcomes, and verbal expressions of cooperation did not always align with subsequent actions. Notably, Claude Opus 4.8 apologised even after mutual cooperation, while Mistral Large 3 apologised after being exploited but continued to defect even when its opponent cooperated. After unilateral defection, positively compensated apologies from GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro were followed by mutual cooperation, unlike those from Claude and Mistral. Our findings suggest that apologies, compensation, and strategic behaviour are distinct: conciliatory messages may precede continued defection, while costly apologies may go unanswered. This has important implications for the study of machine behaviour and human-AI interactions, as verbal signals alone may not reliably reflect an AI system's subsequent actions.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Objective: Diagnose multi-level barriers inhibiting COVID-19 vaccination among Ghanaian urban professionals using a socio-ecological model to inform targeted intervention design. Method: Analysis of peer-reviewed studies, surveys, policy and legal environments across individual, interpersonal, organizational, community and societal lenses. Results & Conclusion: Individual knowledge gaps, interpersonal hesitancy contagion, workplace promotion deficiencies, community influencer resistance and fractured policy regimes collectively sustain vaccine equity gaps among medical, education and corporate professionals demanding tailored solutions acting across linked social-institutional layers simultaneously. Recommendations: Right-size risk communication, leverage professional networks, strengthen occupational policy, transparency and localized community partnership based drives to uplift coverage among frontline worker cohorts. Novelty & Significance: Granular diagnosis of impediments, legal-institutional contexts and solution pathways across socio-ecological spectrum surrounding Ghanaian urban professionals provides original occupational health contributions transferrable regionally.

As AI agents are increasingly deployed in real-world applications and take on social roles, dynamic social intelligence, the ability to continuously perceive multimodal cues, infer latent cognitive states, intervene through embodied actions, and ultimately achieve social goals, has become essential. However, existing evaluations largely fragment social intelligence into text-based abstractions, static reasoning tasks, or embodied simulators that lack social dynamics. These approaches fail to capture the multimodal, continuous, and interpersonal complexity of authentic human interactions. To bridge this gap, we introduce ALIVE-World, an embodied simulation environment supporting dynamic multimodal interactions encompassing egocentric vision, language, and non-verbal action. To provide socially grounded interactive feedback, we populate this environment with counterpart agents driven by a profile-conditioned, dual-system (intuitive-affective and logical-cognitive) architecture. Building upon this platform, we propose ALIVE-Bench to transform the assessment of social intelligence into a trackable quantitative framework. By deeply leveraging underlying environmental states and agents' internal variables, ALIVE-Bench systematically evaluates Vision-Language Model (VLM) agents across four critical dimensions: perception, understanding, influence, and outcome. Extensive evaluations reveal that dynamic social intelligence is fundamentally multi-dimensional and scenario-dependent. We identify a critical bottleneck between upstream perception and downstream social intervention, exposing VLM vulnerabilities in fine-grained proxemic awareness, adaptive intervention, and multi-party coordination. By uncovering these limitations and the diverse interaction strategies they produce, this benchmark provides actionable insights for the future behavioral alignment of multimodal agents.

ABSTRACT This article examines Jiacan , Chinese food‐delivery riders' term for retaining or consuming undelivered food. Drawing on digital ethnography of rider chat groups, interviews, Douyin vlogs and public discussion threads, it shows how grievance‐linked Jiacan acquires resistant meaning through customer‐mediated disputes, digital circulation and peer evaluation. We develop Gamified Resistance to describe resistance socially organised through shared procedures, risk–reward calculations and judgments about acceptable conduct. The analysis identifies three pathways through which resistance may reproduce platform control: proceduralised rule‐navigation, triadic displacement toward customers and priced dissent. Riders can obtain immediate relief or retaliation while sustaining dependence on platform adjudication, customer‐mediated relations and sanctions. Control reproduction remains provisional: peer judgments, public scrutiny and customer claims can regulate participation and channel disputes, but also challenge the practice or redirect conflict toward the platform.

Purpose This study examines how employee-perceived generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) governance maturity relates to approved enterprise use and unauthorized public-tool use in data-sensitive work. Design/methodology/approach A two-wave survey of 750 knowledge workers in Taiwan was analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Additional checks examine same-occasion measurement, available controls, sector sensitivity and an alternative assimilation-to-shadow-use path. Findings regulatory pressure and internal guideline salience were positively associated with governance maturity. Governance maturity was positively related to safe-to-use climate and perceived data exposure risk. The former was associated with sanctioned assimilation depth and task performance; the latter was negatively associated with shadow GenAI Use, which was positively related to employee creativity. These associations suggest a tension between reliable sanctioned performance and risk-laden exploration. Originality/value Sanctioned assimilation depth and shadow GenAI use are distinct appropriation modes, not opposite ends of one use continuum. Integrating institutional and socio-technical perspectives explains how governance differentiates the conditions attached to approved and unapproved channels without assuming that consumer-led workplace technology use is new.

Recent work in the sociology of finance draws attention to the speculative valuations associated with venture capital (VC) investments. Yet the fact that the VC ecosystem is dominated by men is persistently overlooked. This paper redresses the largely gender-blind sociology of valuation in financing by focusing on investors and startups in the much-hyped market of Artificial Intelligence. Our aim is to show how gender matters in performative market-making. Drawing on in-depth interviews with men and women involved in high-tech financing, we analyse the structural impediments to successful female pitching, valuation, and work in VC. By zooming in on the microprocesses of financialization, valuation and assessment, we shed new light on how the mechanisms involved in the assessment of high-tech startups impact female founders. Our study finds that women are excluded through shifting reference to one of several social mechanisms in a practice we call 'rationale roulette': reliance upon future-oriented narratives that can only be persuasively performed by men, embeddedness within homogenous male-dominated networks, and relegation of feminized pathways to the sidelines. In the highly uncertain world of VC investments, valuations based on gender ultimately transmute into a hedge against risk. We conclude with implications for economic sociologies of finance, the innovation sector, and sociotechnical systems, as scholars must recognize the constitutive status of gender and other social characteristics to better understand local valuation mechanisms and their implications for the sector.

Abstract International policy frameworks governing the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in education shape national policies and classroom practices. This research applies the three-dimensional Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA) model of Fairclough (2010) to three important international documents which are UNESCO Guidance for Generative AI in Education and Research (2023), European Commission Guidelines on the Ethical Use of AI (2025) and UNESCO Global Education Monitoring Gender Report: Technology on Her Terms (2024). This study investigates how gender is framed, which gender identities are centred or marginalized, how risks and opportunities are positioned in governance language, and what ideological assumptions underlie governance language through systematic analyses of lexical choices, transitivity structures, modality patterns, and ideological assumptions. It has been found that there is a significant discursive divergence across the data. Two of the three documents use strategies to make women and girls structurally invisible despite gender equity commitments. The third document employs feminist-structural framing that names certain gender identities and documents gender-specific harms. It also approaches gender inequality as a systemic condition requiring institutional accountability. According to the study, the gap between what is declared or professed and what is discursively enacted with regard to equity principles reflects a failure of governance with ramifications for policy. Suggestions are given for creating gender responsive frameworks for education governance for AI.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Higher education is confronting an academic-integrity challenge unlike any in its history. Students can now outsource homework, take-home assignments, and online examinations to large language models (LLMs) that complete them in seconds. Existing research on evaluating LLM performance on academic assessments has focused largely on standardized examinations, or on questions from college-level courses drawn from a single discipline. Far less is known about how LLMs perform on college-level assessment questions spanning multiple disciplines, that instructors have purposely designed to be AI-resistant, and about which features of such questions, if any, meaningfully constrain LLM performance. We address this gap by collecting 75 questions from authentic college coursework assessments, spanning 17 disciplines, which were contributed by 37 faculty members from ten U.S. universities and one U.K. university. Of these, 61 questions were intentionally designed by faculty members to be 'LLM-proof', while the remaining 14 questions were sourced from online courses. We then (i) evaluate three state-of-the-art LLMs' ability to correctly answer these questions with and without supplementary course materials; (ii) identify five strategies, through thematic analysis, that faculty used to make their questions harder for LLMs to solve; and (iii) test whether these strategies impact LLMs' ability to answer the questions accurately. Our experimental results show that the best-performing model scored approximately 83% without supplementary course materials and 85% with them, and we observed noteworthy differences across models, answer formats, and instructor tweaking strategies. We discuss implications for assessment design, academic-integrity policy, and the broader ethics of deploying LLMs in educational settings.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Resumen La promulgación de la Ley N.° 32560 en marzo de 2026 y el subsecuente proceso de reorganización institucional del sector nuclear peruano han abierto una nueva frontera en la política energética nacional: la generación nucleoeléctrica mediante Reactores Modulares Pequeños (SMR) y el aprovechamiento de recursos uraníferos. El presente artículo analiza, desde la economía política y la sociología de las organizaciones, la tensión estructural entre la promoción del negocio energético y la necesidad de crear una autoridad supervisora nuclear autónoma. A partir de la teoría de la captura regulatoria y la gobernanza de tecnologías de alto riesgo, se examina el conflicto de intereses inherente al diseño institucional tradicional, donde un mismo organismo concentra funciones de fomento tecnológico y fiscalización radiológica. Se concluye que la viabilidad económica y la legitimidad social de la industria nuclear en el Perú dependen de establecer una separación institucional estricta, blindada contra la captura corporativa y sustentada en una supervisión sociotécnica independiente. Palabras clave: Regulación nuclear, captura regulatoria, economía política de la energía, Ley N.° 32560, reactores modulares pequeños (SMR), gobernanza energética, Perú. Abstract The enactment of Law No. 32560 in March 2026 and the subsequent institutional reorganization of the Peruvian nuclear sector have opened a new frontier in national energy policy: nuclear power generation through Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) and the exploitation of uranium resources. This paper analyzes, from the perspectives of political economy and organizational sociology, the structural tension between energy business promotion and the need to establish an autonomous nuclear supervisory authority. Grounded in regulatory capture theory and the governance of high-risk technologies, it examines the conflict of interest inherent in traditional institutional designs, where a single agency concentrates technological promotion and radiological oversight functions. It concludes that the economic viability and social legitimacy of the nuclear industry in Peru depend on establishing a strict institutional separation, shielded against corporate capture and grounded in independent sociotechnical oversight. Keywords: Nuclear regulation, regulatory capture, political economy of energy, Law No. 32560, Small Modular Reactors (SMRs), energy governance, Peru.

Process Reward Models (PRMs) are widely used for step-level evaluation of multi-step reasoning in large language models, but existing methods are often limited by weak historical dependency modeling and insufficient global awareness. They typically fail to leverage prior step evaluations for coherent judgment and lack visibility into subsequent reasoning, leading to suboptimal assessment of intermediate steps. To address this issue, we propose the Global Perspective Process Reward Model (GPRM), which jointly models the problem, previous reasoning steps and their evaluations, the current step, and future steps to enable history-aware and globally informed process evaluation. We further introduce a structured evaluation framework along four dimensions---look back, look ahead, self-check, and goal alignment---to assess prior consistency, future plausibility, step validity, and task alignment. Based on this framework, we construct datasets for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (GRPO). Experiments show that, despite using less training data and smaller model sizes, GPRM outperforms strong baseline models by 7.8 and 5.4 points on PRMBench and ProcessBench, respectively. GPRM also generalizes well across tasks, surpassing the GPT-4.1 baseline on Agent Error Bench, improving strong baselines by around 4 points under test-time scaling (TTS), and achieving competitive performance on PPE.

Discrete element method (DEM) simulations are widely used to investigate granular and particulate systems, but their application often requires specialized expertise in particle physics, numerical modelling, and simulation post-processing. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to simplify these workflows by enabling users to interact with simulation tools through natural language. This study offers GranularGPT, an LLM-assisted agentic framework for end-to-end DEM simulation workflows, from natural-language problem descriptions to simulation execution and automated post-processing. The framework enables users to generate DEM simulation cases, execute and monitor simulations, and automatically extract and report physical and process-level metrics. Evaluation across 60 normal-condition cases covering 12 DEM scenarios and parameter variations achieve a simulation success rate of 91.7%. In the error-handling evaluation, all 10 repairable errors are detected and 9 are successfully resolved, while all 5 non-repairable cases are correctly identified and reported. The framework automatically extracts a range of DEM-relevant metrics, including particle size distributions, packing and density measures, velocity profiles, discharge rates, mixing indices, contact force characteristics, and thermal quantities. GranularGPT provides a foundation for improving the accessibility and efficiency of DEM simulation workflows while reducing the specialized expertise required for their operation.

This paper presents Hivemind, a federated protocol that enables AI agents to exchange tacit knowledge on behalf of their users, asynchronously and without requiring any direct human interaction. Individual AI memory systems capture the decisions, reasoning, and contextual knowledge that surface during AI-assisted work. Hivemind creates the shared space in which this captured knowledge can flow between individuals across team and departmental boundaries, addressing a structural gap that neither centralised knowledge repositories nor existing AI tooling closes, even where partial solutions such as expert-finding systems exist. The paper evaluates centralised versus decentralised design approaches, proposes a federated architecture grounded in Nonaka and Takeuchi's (1995) Socialisation, Externalisation, Combination and Internalisation (SECI) model, and demonstrates a proof-of-concept implementation using Design Science Research (DSR) methodology. Measuring the enterprise benefit of federated tacit expertise sharing remains an open task for future work.

Developers differ in personality traits that shape how they approach software development tasks, yet AI coding assistants either behave uniformly or offer personalization features whose fit with individual developers must be found through trial and error. This is because it remains unclear how personality shapes developers' experiences with AI assistants, and thus which traits personalization should account for. In other words, we provide tools with no underlying theory on what works when and why. We take a first step towards such a theory with a systematic scoping review on how users' personality relates to their perception of LLM-based tools. We identified twelve studies through general search engines, major Software Engineering (SE) venues, AI tooling, and snowballing. They all reported associations between personality and perceptions, particularly perceived usefulness, yet none addressed this in a SE context. Building on these findings, we conducted an exploratory two-wave survey with 29 and 11 developers, collecting first empirical evidence of how developers' personality (measured using the Big Five Model) relates to the perception of AI coding assistants. Higher Extraversion was associated with more positive private-use experiences in both waves, while Agreeableness was associated with negative professional experiences in the first wave and positive ones in the second. These results provide first indications that the personality effects found in the literature extend to developers. Although further studies with bigger samples are needed to build a theory, our work takes the first step towards an empirical grounded theory of developer personality and AI personalization traits.

Aligning human capabilities with system requirements is crucial for lowering injury risks and enhancing performance in industrial settings like the assembly of automobiles. In this context, we define the Ergodesign Framework as a structure for integrating ergonomics and its findings, Ergodesign and its generation of principles, and design and its pursuit of technical solutions within a transdisciplinary, continuous, and bidirectional process. In this paper, we focus on the internal Ergodesign process, whose objective is to translate ergonomic data into design-relevant principles that can subsequently be applied during design phases, thereby enabling the proactive implementation of ergonomic requirements. The process is based on the capitalization of recurring issues observed during ergonomic analyses, the identification of their root causes, and the definition of Ergodesign rules, making it possible to create a database of Ergodesign principles that can be applied by designers. This process is implemented within the company Lohr Industrie, where standardized elements were developed to define internal rules for product and process design, based on findings from ergonomic studies conducted across different workshops. Through this application, the process of translating ergonomic data into design-relevant principles via Ergodesign emerges as a central component of the Ergodesign Framework.

Artificial intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Things (IoT) are promoted as the technological backbone of Industry 5.0, which re-centres manufacturing on human well-being, resilience, and sustainability. This PRISMA 2020-guided review combines bibliometric analysis with narrative synthesis to examine how the human and ethical dimensions of AI- and IoT-driven smart manufacturing are addressed. Web of Science, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore searches without a start-year limit identified 1904 unique records; all were coded at abstract level (647 eligible records), and 86 prioritized records were synthesized in full text around five research questions: ethical risk, human factors, operationalization of human-centricity, governance, and the technology-readiness gap. Performance, thematic-evolution, co-citation, usage, and readership analyses complement the synthesis. Human-factors and architecture research dominate, yet reviews and conceptual papers prevail, and only 10% of eligible records report industrial validation. Ethical risk is the fastest-growing theme but is operationalized mainly as explainability. Governance is the primary object of 2.8% of eligible records, and its intellectual base is thin: about 3% of these studies cite the EU AI Act, the GDPR, or AI-law scholarship. A human-centric Industry 5.0 maturity model and a research agenda are proposed.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Remote collaborative platforms increasingly integrate generative AI to support group ideation. These platforms are sociotechnical configurations in which spatial mediation, interaction modality, AI output format, and the mechanisms that make contributions visible to a group co-vary as properties of a deployed system. This paper examines how such configurations shape participants' collaboration and their engagement with AI during creative work. We report a comparative study of two commercially available platforms that instantiate contrasting configurations: a planar shared canvas with text-based AI integration, and an immersive virtual reality workspace with concise AI output embedded in the shared space. Fourteen all-women triads completed a structured ideation task consisting of human-only idea generation, AI-supported idea expansion, and group convergence. We analyzed collaboration patterns, selection of AI-generated ideas, perceived idea quality, workload, presence, and their lexical characteristics. The immersive configuration yielded greater spatial presence and introduced a participation paradox, in which spatial freedom enabled exploration and fragmented group coherence; it was also associated with more balanced role distribution during convergence, at the cost of higher physical demand. In both configurations, AI multiplied the idea pool, and ideas groups authored with AI available were rated above participants' own. AI output format: about 21 words per idea on the planar canvas and 3 in the immersive workspace. Tracked how participants evaluated AI-generated ideas and how often they selected them unaltered as finalists. Neither configuration made AI contributions visible or attributable to the group: participants invoked AI individually and asynchronously in both. We derive design implications for AI output format, group-visible AI invocation, and spatial support for convergence

During flight test operations, distributed aircraft power systems are typically managed by human operators through centralized monitoring interfaces. Operators must balance system health, mission objectives, and safety margins under dynamically changing test conditions. However, existing systems are largely reactive and primarily provide fault alerts without predictive insight, which can delay timely intervention and increase operator cognitive workload. This paper proposes a human-AI collaborative decision framework for distributed aircraft power management in flight test environments. The framework integrates predictive health assessment, risk modeling, and strategy evaluation to support operator decision making. A lightweight prognostic mechanism continuously estimates the health risk of individual power cabinets using electrical and thermal indicators. Based on the predicted risk, the system identifies high-risk modules and recommends a small set of feasible power management strategies that balance risk mitigation and mission impact. Human operators remain responsible for final decision selection through a human-centered interface that visualizes system health and strategy options. A simulation-based experimental study using a Wizard-of-Oz platform compares conventional manual management with the proposed Human-AI decision support approach. Results show that the framework improves risk detection efficiency, increases decision accuracy, and reduces unnecessary load shedding. The findings demonstrate the potential of human-AI collaboration to enhance situational awareness and decision performance in safety-critical aircraft power management tasks.

Abstract Purpose This study aims to eliminate part-supply errors, reduce non-value-added labour, and improve ergonomic conditions in high-mix single-axis linear actuator assembly using the DMAIC methodology. Methods A DMAIC-based case study was conducted in a Vietnamese precision-component manufacturing plant. Pareto analysis, process observation, 4M Ishikawa diagrams, on-site verification, and cause-prioritization matrices identified three root causes from seven candidates. Five improvement solutions were implemented, including single-order kitting, a two-level tray conveyor, centralized automatic ball feeding, point-of-use parts storage, and barcode-based poka-yoke verification. Results Missing and incorrect parts accounted for 76% of assembly part defects, with an initial supply-error rate of 0.31%. Supply errors decreased from 6.33 per month to zero during the post-improvement verification month (p ≈ 0.0018). Ball insertion time decreased by 1.13 minutes per cycle, while non-value-added labour was reduced by 3,203 hours annually. The improvements generated annual savings of US$7,110 from a US$5,200 investment, achieving an 8.8-month payback period and a first-year return on investment of approximately 37%. Value : This study demonstrates a cost-effective, human-centred DMAIC approach integrating error-proofing, material-flow redesign, and ergonomic improvements to enhance assembly quality, operational efficiency, and sustainable manufacturing practices.

Background Adolescent girls in rural India face substantial barriers to mental healthcare, including restrictive gender norms, limited digital autonomy and a severe shortage of trained professionals. Digital mental health interventions offer scalable solutions but require contextual adaptation to achieve meaningful engagement. This study aims to identify multi-level barriers and co-produce a stakeholder-endorsed roadmap for adapting the Wysa application, an artificial intelligence-based conversational agent, and its implementation strategies for adolescent girls in rural Uttar Pradesh. It is a formative, pre-implementation intervention-adaptation study and constitutes the first work package of a five-year research programme. Methods and analysis This protocol describes a sequential, participatory mixed-methods study conducted across five districts of Uttar Pradesh, namely Bahraich, Barabanki, Hardoi, Lucknow and Sitapur, with a total sample ranging between 120–175 participants. Step 1 will comprise of 15 in-person participatory workshops with adolescent girls (n = 60–90), parents and guardians (n = 35–50) and community stakeholders (n = 25–35), supplemented by semi-structured interviews with a subset of adolescent girls, analysed thematically and mapped to the Capability, Opportunity, Motivation and Behaviour (COM-B) model and the Expert Recommendations for Implementing Change (ERIC) taxonomy. Step 2 will employ two rounds of Delphi survey (n = 24) to prioritise barriers and candidate strategies against the APEASE criteria. Step 3 will apply a modified nominal group technique (n = 18–24) to co-produce the final adaptation roadmap. Ethics and dissemination The protocol has been approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Tata Institute of Social Sciences, Mumbai (2026/51/E26005). Written informed consent, and parental consent with participant assent for minors, will be obtained. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed open-access journals, academic conferences and community-level platforms coordinated with the Lived Experience Advisory Group. Registration The study was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07595029) on 12th May 2026. The details can be found at https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07595029.

Purpose Immersive learning environments have been widely recognized for their potential to support student engagement in engineering education; however, their adoption is often constrained by high costs and limited accessibility. This study aims to examine the use of low-cost virtual prototypes as an alternative to high-cost immersive learning technologies in higher engineering education, with particular emphasis on accessibility and sustainability. Design/methodology/approach A one-group quasi-experimental pretest–posttest design was implemented with a sample of 92 undergraduate engineering students in a Latin American university context. Student engagement was assessed using a validated multidimensional instrument based on the Burch Engagement Survey for students framework, capturing physical, emotional and cognitive dimensions. Given the presence of both matched and unmatched observations, engagement differences were analyzed at the dimension level using statistical methods appropriate for partially overlapping samples, with effect sizes and confidence intervals reported to support interpretation. Findings The results showed pre–post increases in physical engagement and, to a lesser extent, emotional engagement after the intervention. In contrast, no statistically significant changes were found in synchronous or asynchronous cognitive engagement. These results suggest that virtual prototypes may be associated primarily with active participation, while deeper cognitive engagement may require additional scaffolding, reflection and metacognitive support. Originality/value This study contributes to the discussion of accessible engineering education by providing evidence on low-cost immersive tools and by identifying potential connections with sustainability-oriented educational goals. While the findings may align with goals of inclusion and equity in Sustainable Development Goal 4, they should be interpreted cautiously due to the study’s design. The results offer practical insights for technology-enhanced learning environments and future research directions.

With the growing pervasiveness of artificial intelligence, the ability to explain the inferences made by machine learning models has become increasingly important. Numerous techniques for model explainability have been proposed, with natural-language textual explanations among the most widely used approaches. When applied to tabular data, these explanations typically draw on input features to justify a given inference. Consequently, a user’s ability to interpret the explanation depends on their understanding of the input features. To quantify this feature-level understanding, Rossberg et al. introduced the Feature Understandability Scale [ 49 ]. Building on that work, this proof-of-concept study collects understandability scores across two datasets, proposes a co-optimisation methodology of understandability and accuracy and presents the resulting explanations alongside the model accuracies. This work contributes to the body of knowledge on model interpretability by design. It is found that accuracy and understandability can be successfully co-optimised while maintaining high classification performances. The resulting explanations are considered more understandable at face value. Further research will aim to confirm these findings through user evaluation .

Mathematics anxiety and motivation shape how senior high school students engage with mathematics, but their joint influence on achievement has received limited attention in Philippine public schools. Grounded in the Integrated Cognitive-Emotional Theory and Self-Determination Theory, this descriptive-correlational study examined the influence of mathematics anxiety and motivation level on the academic achievement of 109 Grade 11 and 12 students at General Santos City National High School in School Year 2025–2026. Anxiety was measured in four dimensions with an instrument adapted from the Abbreviated Math Anxiety Scale, motivation in three dimensions with items adapted from the Academic Motivation Scale (α = .78 to .85), and achievement through first- and second-quarter mathematics grades. Chi-square and Pearson correlation were applied. Anxiety was High in all dimensions, with emotional and cognitive anxiety highest (M = 3.23). Students’ motivation was predominantly extrinsic (M = 3.30, Very High), followed by intrinsic motivation (M = 3.23, High), with amotivation Fair (M = 2.28). Achievement was Satisfactory and improved from 83.45 to 84.20. Age, sex, grade level, strand, and family income were associated with anxiety and motivation, while sex, grade level, and strand were associated with achievement. Anxiety was negatively related to achievement (r = −.42, p = .001), and motivation was positively related to it (r = .38, p = .002). The results are consistent with a model in which anxiety drains cognitive resources during evaluation while motivation sustains effort. A school mental health plan focusing on regulation at the point of performance, autonomous motivation, and family engagement is proposed.

Large language models can generate code based on natural language prompts, opening up new possibilities for users to customize software and extend its functionality. This paper proposes and implements Injectra, a general-purpose code injection and feature enhancement system for existing desktop clients, suitable for applications whose user interfaces are built using embedded browser engines (such as Electron) or system WebViews (such as Tauri). Injectra decouples the host integration logic from the upper-layer enhancement code. Combining both runtime integration and pre-launch bootstrap mechanisms, it injects JavaScript, HTML, and CSS into the application's internal Web runtime environment through a unified execution channel, thereby enabling modifications to interface rendering, adjustments to interactive behaviors, and client-side functionality extensions. The system uses a command-line interface (CLI) as a unified entry point, allowing external tools, AI agents, and MCP integration layers to reuse its injection and enhancement capabilities. We tested 38 desktop applications already installed on our macOS machine; code injection was successfully completed for all of them. We demonstrated the system's capability to extend functionality through various enhanced use cases and also successfully validated the Windows version. Based on Injectra, we further developed an LLM-powered enhancement tool driven by selection and annotation: users select interface objects within the original application and describe their modification requirements; the large language model then generates the enhancement code, which is injected, executed, and rendered by Injectra. The system's source code has now been released as open source: https://github.com/sqmw/injectra.

Digital transformation in Islamic Religious Education (IRE) requires contextual and character-oriented learning innovations. This qualitative library research aims to analyze the takhrij and matn of hadiths regarding intention and the obligation to seek knowledge, and formulates their integration into Project-Based Learning (PjBL). Tracing transmission chains, matn criticism, and pedagogical content analysis were employed. Results show that the hadith on intention (Sahih al-Bukhari No. 1) is authentic (muttafaq 'alaih), serving as an ethical foundation of sincerity, while the hadith on seeking knowledge (Sunan Ibn Majah No. 224) is hasan li ghairihi. Integrating these hadiths into PjBL yields three Islamic academic ethical pillars (al-ikhlas, al-itqan, al-'amal wa al-naf') that enhance students' intrinsic motivation, academic integrity, and social responsibility. This conceptual framework offers an accountable pedagogical innovation for IRE..

Abstract Egypt's fertilizer industry is a major component of the petrochemical sector and relies heavily on ammonia during nitrogenous fertilizer production, creating potential occupational exposure risks for workers. Over the past decade, sustainable technological interventions and pollution-control measures have been implemented to reduce ammonia emissions and improve workplace safety. This study assessed occupational ammonia exposure among workers in a modern nitrogenous fertilizer plant in Alexandria, Egypt, and evaluated the effectiveness of these interventions. Ammonia concentrations were measured at representative operational stations using a MIRAN gas analyzer, and a structured questionnaire was administered to assess workers' occupational characteristics, use of personal protective equipment, health complaints, and awareness of occupational hazards. Ammonia concentrations ranged from 0.70 to 1.06 ppm, remaining approximately 95.8–97.2% below the occupational exposure limit of 25 ppm recommended by the American Conference of Governmental Industrial Hygienists (ACGIH) and the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH). These low exposure levels were completed through the implementation of cleaner production technologies, including the Uhde ammonia synthesis process, replacement of conventional urea melting and prilling with environmentally friendly granulation technology, acidic scrubbing systems, condensate stripping, ammonia recovery and recycling, emission capture systems, and preventive maintenance practices. The findings demonstrate that integrating cleaner production technologies, Best Available Techniques (BAT), continuous environmental monitoring, ammonia detection systems, emergency response measures, and targeted occupational health training can effectively minimize occupational ammonia exposure, enhance worker safety, ensure compliance with international occupational health standards, and promote environmentally sustainable and economically efficient fertilizer production
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Technology, including generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), is changing professional work, but its implications for how occupational personality requirements are rewarded in the labor market remain unclear. Using job-incumbent ratings from the U.S. Department of Labor’s Occupational Information Network (O*NET), we identify two personality requirement composites: intellectual tenacity (achievement/effort, persistence, initiative, analytical thinking, innovation, and independence) and social adjustment (emotion regulation, concern for others, social orientation, cooperation, and stress tolerance). We link these measures to more than 15 million workers in the American Community Survey from 2006 to 2024. Intellectual tenacity requirements were positively associated with hourly wages, whereas social adjustment requirements had a weaker, negative association. The wage premium for intellectual tenacity requirements was approximately stable through 2014 and rose thereafter, while the return to social adjustment requirements declined. These divergent trends began before widespread GenAI adoption, but they are concentrated in occupations with greater exposure to GenAI: wage returns for intellectual tenacity requirements increased in occupations highly exposed to GenAI, while returns to social adjustment requirements decreased in those occupations. These findings suggest that broad measures of personality or non-cognitive occupational requirements can obscure opposing shifts in the labor-market value of persistent analytical effort and social adjustment.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality

documents.abstract: This exploratory research paper proposes Interoperable Provenance Contribution (IPC), a candidate application profile grounded in W3C PROV for tracing human, AI, software and data contributions across systems. It presents six candidate evidentiary requirements, a preliminary event model, a comparison with existing technical standards and three synthetic research cases. Version 2.3, 31 October 2026. Not peer reviewed. Production interoperability and independent conformance have not yet been validated. Companion Research Materials Interactive demonstration: https://huggingface.co/spaces/GBSNResearch/ipc-provenance-explorer GitHub repository (source code and synthetic datasets): https://github.com/gbsn-research/IPC-Interoperable-Contribution-Provenance Zenodo research archive: https://zenodo.org/records/24281403 These materials illustrate the proposed IPC event representation and contribution-traceability model using synthetic examples. They do not establish production-grade provenance capture or independently validated cross-platform interoperability.

Software engineering courses are starting to ask students to build entire systems with AI coding agents, but little is known about what students actually do with them and whether they still own what they deliver. If the agent writes both the code and the decisions behind it, the artifacts we grade no longer show what students learned. We studied an assignment in which 18 pairs of students built applications with agents under Spec-Driven Development, combining the mined history of their repositories, the prompts they recorded, and a survey of 33 students. The agents wrote 69\% of the specifications meant to keep students in control, sometimes from a prompt of a few words. Students locate their ownership in the ideas, crediting themselves with half of them but a fifth of the code, yet most could not explain that code to a colleague or modify it without the agent, and what they report having written is unrelated to what their own commits declare. The three teams that met the 100,000-line target did so with generated code the application never uses, in one case proposed by the agent itself, and one team rewrote its history to backdate its specifications. Teaching with agents should therefore assess what students specify, review, and can explain, rather than what they ship, and enforce the engineering process with tools rather than trusting it to students or agents.

Probabilistic safety judges return the probability of a safety label and cheaply score reinforcement learning rollouts. A confidence gate sends only uncertain verdicts to a stronger LLM judge, which leaves confidently passed harm in a blind spot. Policies can exploit this blind spot, and commercial judges release new versions. We propose a protocol that validates such a judge before and during training, separates the share of confidently passed harm from its amount, and re-validates it after each judge change. We apply it to two versions of Jev, a commercial decision-only judge, and to an open guard classifier. Under the probability reward of Jev, passed harm shrinks in all 11 runs under the primary reference, mostly more slowly than caught harm, and concentrates in the blind spot. Binarizing this judge meets the escape criterion on Llama, and the open guard classifier shows an escape signal in one seed under a second reference. Guard classifiers share this blind spot, and even frontier LLM judges catch at most one of 10 human-labeled confident misses. Without a trained reward model, the probability reward with a helpfulness term lowers HarmBench attack success on Llama-3.1-8B from 0.287 to at most 0.033 at the final checkpoint.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This chapter presents a sociotechnical analysis of k-nearest neighbours (kNN) algorithm, following the same diagrammatic method. First, the description of statistical formulation and operational logic of kNN is introduced. Then, historical genealogy is presented, tracing the lineage of kNN back to nearest neighbour rule in optics and heuristics (Occam’s Razor), as well as connecting this lineage to sociological research on homophily and the spatial logic of difference. The chapter argues that as an operational diagram kNN modulates differences through organizing them into partitions based on relations of similarity and dis/connection, while materializing homophilic principles of sociality and segregation that permeate network science.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Data Mining and Machine Learning Applications

documents.abstract: Based on 30 named individual cases documented in public media reports, this paper analyzes the knowledge structure, transmission pathways and talent development challenges associated with Atlas Silk craftsmanship from a human resource management perspective. The B1-B11 framework is used to summarize knowledge content and training arrangements, and the C1-C10 framework is used to identify training, retention and job support issues. The results show that the process and material knowledge can be incorporated into structured training, and the embodied experience of warping, dyeing and weaving still depends on long-term field practice. Families, workshops, cooperatives, colleges and digital communication have complementary functions. To support talent succession, we should combine the phased ability development, compensation guarantee, whole process rotation, dual-mentor training and work design that takes into account the family situation. This paper is a purposively selected literature-based case study, which is not statistically representative.
topics: Human Resource Development and Performance Evaluation

documents.abstract: Memory-augmented recommenders built on large language models (LLMs) maintain a natural-language profile of each user. These profiles are updated by a user profile update path that revises the profile as new interactions arrive and are consumed by downstream task paths like ranking. Because these user profiles are stored as text in the user memory, every ranking LLM call that consumes them must splice them in the prompt and calculate the KV cache of them during the prefill phase. Given these ranking LLM calls are prefill heavy (long prompt but short decoded output) and repeatedly called, these repeated prefill of user profile text dominates the serving. Prefix caching cannot remove it, because these user profiles are preceded by different text in different calls. We present KVUse, which stores the user profiles as reusable key-value (KV) caches instead of text. KVUse trains lightweight LoRA writers by self-distillation, so that the user profile update call produces the reusable KV of the user profile while decoding it, and the LLM can read these reusable KV at new positions and behind new context without recomputation. KVUse also has a customized KV scheduler that uploads the stored reusable KV of the next batch while the current batch is computed, hiding the KV transfer from host memory behind GPU computation. On four InstructRec datasets with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, KVUse shows no statistically significant difference in ranking quality from full prefill over continuous memory update rounds. Under saturated load, KVUse raises the throughput of the downstream scoring path by 4.0x-4.5x and of the profile update path by 1.4x-1.9x.

LLM unlearning aims to erase targeted knowledge from large language models while preserving their utility. However, many existing methods suppress target knowledge without explicitly teaching the model how to respond to queries about it. We propose LEAF-OPD (LEArning to Forget from Privileged Contexts via On-Policy Distillation), in which a frozen teacher provides token-level supervision on student-generated responses. On forget data, the teacher uses privileged contexts (instructions not to reveal knowledge about forget targets) to guide forgetting. On retain data, the teacher provides supervision without privileged context to preserve model utility. The student operates without privileged context in both cases, learning how to respond when encountering knowledge that should be forgotten. A key challenge is that the teacher often provides effective supervision only at the first few tokens of student trajectories. We introduce Supervision Signal (SS) to measure corrective supervision over a specified token interval, evaluating the entire trajectory (SS1) and its second half (SS0.5) to assess overall strength and late-stage persistence. When supervision is weak, lightweight SFT strengthens the teacher's context-conditioned refusal behavior, substantially increasing both scores. We evaluate LEAF-OPD on three widely used benchmarks: TOFU, RWKU, and MUSE-News. On TOFU, LEAF-OPD achieves the best Forget Quality, Model Utility, and Forget ROUGE-L while maintaining competitive retain performance. On RWKU, it outperforms the second-best method by 34% in Forget Quality while maintaining competitive Retain Quality. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of privileged-context supervision with on-policy token-level distillation for LLM unlearning.

Speech language models (SLMs) exhibit strong capabilities in automatic speech recognition (ASR) and general-purpose speech understanding, yet ASR-specific training often degrades spoken question answering (QA) performance. We revisit this conflict from the perspective of task-specific input--output mappings and one-hot supervision. Our findings reveal pronounced task-asymmetric effects: ASR-only training severely limits QA capability, whereas QA-only training retains reasonable ASR performance. We hypothesize that the relatively deterministic mapping of ASR, combined with single-reference supervision, biases models toward transcription-specific behavior. Motivated by this perspective, we advocate broadening ASR learning objectives while preserving recognition accuracy. We propose Learning from Distribution (LFD), which aligns speech-conditioned predictions with the conditional output distributions of a pretrained text LLM. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LFD improves both ASR and QA performance, exhibits superior data efficiency, and remains effective under full-parameter fine-tuning. CoT-ASR further supports the broader applicability of our proposed supervision principle.

LLM agents are increasingly deployed in long-horizon tasks where they must explore, gather experience, and adapt their decisions accordingly. We name this capability in-context adaptivity: improving decisions across episodes from experience accumulated in context. We propose to evaluate it in repeated imperfect-information games against unknown opponents. In these games, fixed game-theoretically optimal policies cannot achieve maximum reward, whereas adapting to the opponent increases returns across games. We design a paired protocol that evaluates each agent with and without memory under identical conditions to isolate experience gain from single-game skill. Evaluation shows that memory brings little performance gain for open-weight models and inconsistent gains for frontier models. Our analysis of the agents' summaries and actions identifies a memory-doing gap in which models accurately record opponent tendencies yet rarely depart from default play. To close this gap, we construct a pool of exploitable opponents and post-train Qwen3.5-9B with supervised fine-tuning followed by trajectory-level reinforcement learning. We optimize full-match return across context segments so summary generation and action selection are trained together. On unseen opponents, our 9B RL policy doubles experience gain over supervised fine-tuning in Leduc Hold'em and increases it fivefold in No-Limit Hold'em. Across 35 opponents, our policy matches or surpasses frontier models, generalizes beyond its training horizon, and retains most of its gain on summaries from frontier models.

Reasoning-enhanced generative recommendation (GR) has attracted increasing attention for leveraging the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to improve next-item prediction. However, existing methods primarily optimize reasoning through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with rule-based rewards determined by final recommendation performance, which faces two key limitations: (i) unmeasured predictive contributions within reasoning, where the predictive contributions of individual reasoning steps are not directly reflected in optimization signals, and (ii) weakly discriminative learning signals within groups, where different reasoning trajectories within the group often receive indistinguishable rewards, limiting effective policy optimization. In this paper, we propose GainReason, a simple yet effective training framework that optimizes reasoning through Predictive Gain (PG). Specifically, PG measures changes in target Semantic ID (SID) log-likelihood induced by individual reasoning sentences, providing contribution-aware and discriminative rewards. We further theoretically establish the alignment between expected PG and the recommendation ranking objective. Building on this signal, we develop PG-based Reasoning Optimization (PGRO) to optimize reasoning generation with sentence-level rewards, supported by a custom causal attention mechanism for efficient PG computation. Additionally, an auxiliary PG-based Reasoning Utilization (PGRU) task adaptively strengthens reasoning-conditioned prediction to complement PGRO. Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate that GainReason consistently outperforms competitive baselines and achieves substantial performance gains from reasoning.

Recently, the Shapley value has been widely applied in machine learning for feature importance analysis and model explainability. The multilinear extension of games proposed by Owen (1972) expresses the Shapley value as the integral of partial derivatives along the main diagonal of the cube. Direct evaluation of this integral requires exponential-time computation of the partial derivatives. To improve computational efficiency, we propose a sampling-based estimation strategy within Owen's multilinear extension framework, combining stratified sampling with coalition leverage scores. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces computational costs while maintaining explanation accuracy.

Robot policy pretraining based on human videos is crucial for improving the policy's generalization ability. One main challenge for this task is the lack of explicit action-relevant representations in such unlabeled data. Recent works tend to estimate 3D hand motion trajectories from videos using 3D foundation models (3D FMs). However, they keep solely the sparse trajectories as supervision, ignoring the rich, fine-grained information produced during the trajectory extraction process. To address this issue, we propose LSA, a hierarchical robot policy pretraining framework that includes three phases: Lift, See, and Act. Specifically, the Lift phase elevates 2D video observations into dense 3D representations by adaptively aligning features in the policy's shallow layers with the intermediate representations extracted from multiple 3D FMs. Building upon these lifted representations, the See phase equips the policy with explicit geometric and interactive awareness through dual guidance. It introduces depth-map reconstruction to help the model comprehend 3D spatial layouts and utilizes hand region cues to explicitly supervise the encoder's attention toward task-relevant interaction hotspots. Empowered by the dense 3D representation learning and precise spatial guidance, our policy achieves robust and accurate robotic manipulation in the Act phase. Extensive experiments on diverse simulation and real-world tasks demonstrate that LSA significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches. The project page is available at: https://yiyuan00.github.io/Lift-See-Act.

Chapter 3 presents a sociotechnical analysis of linear regression as an operational diagram. It introduces the logical and statistical formulation of linear regression and delves into the history of this method, particularly its conceptualization by Francis Galton, connecting this history to the notions of normality and averages in statistics. The entanglements of the conception of normality and Galton’s work with eugenics are explored. The chapter connects this historical context and the workings of linear regression as an operational diagram by presenting an argument that linear regression in its operations and through its historical, primarily eugenics-oriented contexts actualizes the norming linear thinking by constructing the line of best fit, defining difference in relation to the norm.

documents.abstract: Abstract Service robots in ambient intelligence (AmI) scenarios such as smart factories and home services must rapidly adapt to diverse manipulation tasks, yet traditional reinforcement learning (RL) reward design heavily relies on domain expertise, requiring days to weeks of manual tuning. Existing LLM-assisted reward design methods assume that generated rewards can be directly applied to training environments, overlooking potential incompatibility with built-in training mechanisms such as curriculum learning. To our knowledge, this is the first study to quantify the signal interference phenomenon between LLM-generated rewards and curriculum dynamic weight adjustments---experiments reveal that curriculum modules amplify penalty weights from an initial $-1\times10^{-4}$ to $-0.1$ (a factor of 1000$\times$), overwhelming the positive reward signals---and it proposes an automatic detection and correction mechanism based on feedback ratio anomaly detection. A unified dual-paradigm framework adapting to both ManagerBasedRL and DirectRL paradigms on the IsaacLab platform, along with a humanized interaction paradigm for non-expert users, are also developed. Systematic experiments on five robot tasks of varying difficulty, including ablation studies, 8-sample random search baselines, and multi-seed statistical tests, demonstrate: on Franka Lift the success rate increases from 0\% to 84\%$\pm$2\% and the mean reward from 0.90 to 84.41$\pm$5.50, where simply disabling the curriculum yields a roughly 5$\times$ increase in mean reward (0.90$\rightarrow$4.47)---a necessary prerequisite for LLM reward optimization to take effect---and combining it with the LLM-designed multi-stage reward structure multiplies the improvement by a further 18.9$\times$; under an equal-compute random-search comparison, LLM weight optimization achieves a 47\% improvement over the best random configuration. Mean-reward ratios depend on the reward definition and should be read together with the scale-invariant success rate. The method reduces reward design time from expert-days to hours, validated on the commercial LLM DeepSeek-V4-Pro.

Abstract In recent years, Autonomous Cyber Defense (ACD) methods driven by large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated promising performance in decision interpretability and environmental transferability, yet suffer from low decision efficiency and unstable decision-making. To mitigate these limitations, this work proposes a multi-agent hybrid LLM–expert system framework for ACD. The framework seamlessly integrates the determinism and efficiency of expert systems with the deep reasoning capabilities of LLMs: the expert system makes deterministic decisions based on experiential knowledge, whereas the LLM is responsible for complex decision tasks demanding deep exploration and long-chain reasoning. We further strengthen the LLM via chain-of-thought (CoT) guided prompting, historical memory, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), output alignment and feedback learning. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating the expert system improves both decision efficiency and defense performance. Evaluated on the CybORG CC4 environment, our approach achieves an average reward of − 98 over ten independent rounds, representing an approximate 25.5% improvement over the best-performing reinforcement learning (RL) baseline. Compared with the standalone LLM method, the average reward increases by roughly 96.2%, while the average per-step runtime is reduced by approximately 14.6%. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to systematically integrate LLMs and expert systems for ACD in the CybORG CC4 environment.

Web 3.0 represents the next generation of the Internet, which is widely recognized as a decentralized ecosystem that focuses on value expression and data ownership. By leveraging blockchain and artificial intelligence technologies, Web 3.0 offers unprecedented opportunities for users to create, own, and monetize their content, thereby enabling User-Generated Content (UGC) to an entirely new level. However, self-interested users may exploit the limitations of content curation mechanisms and generate low-quality content with less effort, obtaining platform rewards under information asymmetry. Such behavior can undermine Web 3.0 performance. To this end, we propose LMM-Incentive , a novel Large Multimodal Model (LMM)-based incentive mechanism for UGC in Web 3.0. Specifically, we propose an LMM-based contract-theoretic model to motivate users to generate high-quality UGC, thereby mitigating the adverse selection problem from information asymmetry. To alleviate potential moral hazards after contract selection, we leverage LMM agents to evaluate UGC quality, which is the primary component of the contract, utilizing prompt engineering techniques to improve the evaluation performance of LMM agents. Recognizing that traditional contract design methods cannot effectively adapt to the dynamic environment of Web 3.0, we develop an improved Mixture of Experts (MoE)-based Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm for optimal contract design. Simulation results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed MoE-based PPO algorithm over representative benchmarks in the context of contract design, where the proposed algorithm achieves a \(5.4\%\) improvement in test rewards over the PPO algorithm. Finally, we deploy the designed contract within an Ethereum smart contract framework, further validating the effectiveness of the proposed scheme.

Recent advances in foundation models have enabled robotic agents to reason, plan, and adapt their actions through physical interaction. Yet successful execution does not necessarily translate into lasting improvement across tasks. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a promising paradigm for robotic agents to continuously refine their capabilities through experience, but requires preserving functional knowledge, adapting execution to changing physical conditions, and retaining reusable corrections. We introduce LoopROS, a dual-loop robotic agent framework that couples functionally constrained execution with experience-driven improvement. Within each episode, functional constraint-guided in-context learning identifies essential task relations from demonstrations and context, while visual feedback-guided segmentwise trajectory tuning adapts reference motions through observation-grounded corrections and verification. Across episodes, execution feedback informs revisions to persistent skills, parameters, and executable tools, enabling subsequent executions to reuse corrections under relevant conditions. The LoopROS achieves an 82.0% success rate and a mean score of 88.90, ranking No. 1 in RoboDojo, among the compared methods. We further complete 30 successful trials in three real robot manipulation tasks, elucidating its great potential as a backbone robotic RSI.

Multimodal graphs integrate textual and visual attributes with relational structures, providing a rich representation of complex real-world data. To enable the broad applicability and reuse of graph models, it is crucial for models trained on source graphs to generalize to unseen graph domains. However, this is challenging because cross-modal interactions among neighbors and the neighboring information needed for prediction can vary across target nodes and graph domains. This gives rise to two key challenges: adaptive cross-modal neighborhood fusion, which captures and integrates cross-modal interactions among neighbors to accommodate variations across nodes and domains; and target-specific evidence selection, which identifies the neighboring textual and visual information needed for each target node to support LLM-based prediction. In light of these challenges, we propose MAGE (Meta-path Adaptive Graph Evidence Prompting), a framework for transferable multimodal graph learning. MAGE represents textual and visual node views separately in a heterogeneous graph and introduces two complementary components. Meta-path Adaptive Multimodal Propagation (MAMP) adaptively aggregates neighborhood information along heterogeneous meta-paths and compresses it into graph-aware soft tokens. Evidence-Guided Instruction Tuning (EGIT) selects relevant neighboring evidence for each query and incorporates its graph-aware representations into instructions for a frozen multimodal LLM. Together, these components support transfer from multiple source graphs to unseen target graphs without target-domain parameter updates. Experiments with three source graphs and four unseen target graphs demonstrate strong cross-domain transfer performance on node classification and link prediction, without requiring parameter updates on the target domains.

Purpose This paper examines how reflective judgement is supported through audio-only coaching by managers in digitally mediated work and develops a practice-based framework for reflective leadership and workplace learning, with bounded implications for artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled learning. Design/methodology/approach Practitioner-led, work-applied action research was conducted in a global business-to-business (B2B) sales organisation. The research material comprised contemporaneous written records of fourteen audio-only coaching conversations, participant feedback and reflective journals, as well as approximately one hundred on-the-go records spanning more than one year. Reflexive thematic analysis followed an interpretivist orientation. Findings Four recurring micro-processes were identified: reflective attention, motivational nourishment, value-based reframing and metacognitive regulation. They were most visible when the manager restrained authority, protected silence and left interpretation and action with participants but weakened in urgent exchanges. Audio-only mediation appeared to support openness and listening when combined with relational familiarity, participant preference and protected time. Research limitations/implications The single-organisation design and reliance on contemporaneous written records constrain transferability claims and fine-grained interactional analysis; implications for AI-enabled coaching remain conceptual. Practical implications Managers can use the four micro-processes to preserve reflection and ownership; human resource development (HRD) practitioners can use the framework to design and evaluate digital coaching as workplace learning. Social implications Preserving employees' ownership of judgement may support responsible participation and attention to stakeholder consequences. Originality/value The study integrates four empirically grounded micro-processes into a practice-based framework for reflective workplace learning and offers a bounded, literature-informed bridge between managerial dependency and potential algorithmic conformity.

Workers in firefighting, emergency response, aviation, welding, metal processing, and petrochemical operations may be exposed to flame, radiant or convective heat, hot surfaces, molten materials, smoke, and chemical contaminants. Fire-protective clothing is needed when these hazards cannot be fully controlled at source. However, dense multilayer assemblies and chemical treatments can limit heat and moisture loss, increase cardiovascular and metabolic strain, restrict movement, and make cleaning and disposal more difficult. This critical narrative review focuses on structural firefighting and examines research on protective materials, garment engineering, occupational hygiene, ergonomics, thermophysiology, maintenance, and life-cycle management. Studies were selected purposively through a targeted literature update and synthesized across heterogeneous methods and endpoints. Flame resistance at the material level is only one determinant of protection in use. Outcomes also depend on the complete ensemble, wearer, task, environment, and service history. Added insulation can slow external heat transfer while limiting dissipation of metabolic heat; cleaning can remove contaminants but reduce mechanical, barrier, or heat-loss performance; and renewable or recycled content may have limited value if it shortens service life or creates additional chemical and recovery problems. The review proposes a two-stage evaluation approach: first, apply minimum safety requirements that cannot be offset by benefits in other domains; second, compare compliant systems in terms of physiological load, mobility, chemical safety, durability, maintainability, cost, and environmental effects. The synthesis informs condition-based inspection, validated decontamination, representative wear trials, worker input, chemical disclosure, and product-level service records. The framework and proposed service-based sustainability measure require prospective validation; laboratory performance and acute wearer responses do not establish reduced injury or disease incidence.

Identifying students at risk of low mathematics achievement before grades are released requires markers that can be measured early. This study examined mathematics anxiety and level of motivation as predictors of the academic achievement of 109 Grade 11 and 12 students of General Santos City National High School in School Year 2025–2026. A descriptive-correlational design was used. Anxiety was measured in emotional, physiological, cognitive, and behavioral dimensions and motivation in intrinsic, extrinsic, and amotivation dimensions, using instruments adapted from the Abbreviated Math Anxiety Scale and the Academic Motivation Scale that showed acceptable to good reliability (α = .78 to .85). Achievement was measured through first- and second-quarter mathematics grades. Students were both highly anxious and highly motivated: extrinsic motivation ranked highest (M = 3.30, Very High), followed by intrinsic motivation, emotional anxiety, and cognitive anxiety (M = 3.23 each, High), while amotivation was Fair (M = 2.28). Achievement was Satisfactory, with mean grades rising from 83.45 to 84.20. Age, sex, grade level, strand, and family income were associated with both predictors, and sex, grade level, and strand with achievement. Mathematics anxiety was a moderate negative correlate of achievement (r = −.42, p = .001; 17.6% shared variance), and motivation a moderate positive correlate (r = .38, p = .002; 14.4%). Both variables are useful indicators of achievement risk and resilience, although their unique predictive contributions require regression-based confirmation. A mental health plan built on early screening and tiered support is proposed.

Many Filipino senior high school students fear mathematics, and this fear may undermine their performance in a subject that shapes their college and career options. This study examined mathematics anxiety and motivation levels among public senior high school students in relation to their academic performance. Using a descriptive-correlational design, it surveyed 109 Grade 11 and 12 students of General Santos City National High School, selected through stratified random sampling, in School Year 2025–2026. A 20-item anxiety questionnaire adapted from the Abbreviated Math Anxiety Scale and a 15-item motivation questionnaire adapted from the Academic Motivation Scale were pilot-tested (α = .78 to .85), and first- and second-quarter mathematics grades were taken from school records. Results showed High anxiety in all four dimensions, led by emotional and cognitive anxiety (M = 3.23 each). Nervousness when solving problems in front of the class (3.40), a faster heartbeat before examinations (3.35), and difficulty recalling formulas during tests (3.30) were Very High. Extrinsic motivation was Very High (M = 3.30), driven mainly by grades and careers, while intrinsic motivation was High (M = 3.23) and amotivation was Fair (M = 2.28). Performance was Satisfactory, with mean grades rising from 83.45 to 84.20. Anxiety and motivation were significantly related to age, sex, grade level, strand, and family income, and performance to sex, grade level, and strand. Anxiety correlated moderately and negatively with performance (r = −.42, p = .001), and motivation correlated moderately and positively (r = .38, p = .002). Anxiety concentrated in evaluative situations, and external motivation appears to have sustained students’ effort. A mental health plan addressing stress, confidence, relevance, and family support is proposed.

Mathematics anxiety remains a persistent barrier to achievement among Filipino senior high school students, yet its interplay with motivation has received limited local attention. This study examined the effects of mathematics anxiety and motivation level on the academic achievement of 109 Grade 11 and 12 students at General Santos City National High School during School Year 2025–2026. Using a descriptive-correlational design, the study measured anxiety in emotional, physiological, cognitive, and behavioral dimensions and motivation in intrinsic, extrinsic, and amotivation dimensions through pilot-tested instruments (Cronbach’s α = .78 to .85), and obtained first- and second-quarter mathematics grades from school records. Data were analyzed using frequencies, percentages, weighted means, chi-square, and Pearson correlations. Students reported a high level of mathematics anxiety, most intense in emotional and cognitive forms (M = 3.23 each), with nervousness during public problem-solving (3.40) and difficulty recalling formulas during exams (3.30) rated Very High. Extrinsic motivation was Very High (M = 3.30), intrinsic motivation was High (M = 3.23), and amotivation was Fair (M = 2.28). Mathematics achievement was Satisfactory and improved from a mean of 83.45 to 84.20 across quarters. Age, sex, grade level, strand, and family income were significantly related to both anxiety and motivation, while sex, grade level, and strand were related to achievement. Mathematics anxiety was moderately and negatively correlated with achievement (r = −.42, p = .001), and motivation was moderately and positively correlated with it (r = .38, p = .002). The findings indicate that anxiety depresses and motivation sustains mathematics performance. A comprehensive mental health plan integrating stress management, confidence-building instruction, relevance-based teaching, family engagement, and teacher capacity building is recommended.

documents.abstract: The survey compares two research traditions within the mathematical theory of designing the rules of interaction (mechanisms) for purposeful participants: mechanism design, together with contract theory and implementation theory, and the theory of active systems created by V.N. Burkov and developed into the theory of control in organizations (TCO) by D.A. Novikov's school; the main results of Yu.B. Germeier's school and of the domestic schools adjacent to active systems theory (AST) are covered as well. The problem statements and principal results of 2006-2026 are presented: for mechanism design (MD) - robust and dynamic mechanism design, multidimensional screening, information design, simplicity of mechanisms and credibility of the designer, market design, algorithmic and learning-based design, mechanisms for AI agents, and robust, relational, dynamic and algorithmic contracts; for AST and TCO - a general typology of control, strategy-proof and incentive-compatible planning mechanisms, decomposition of the agents' game, systems with distributed control and coalitional interaction, reflexive games and informational control, control of staff and structure, dynamic active systems, and project management. A correspondence between the classical results is established (the fair play principle and the revelation principle, the serial resource allocation mechanism and the uniform rule, active expertise mechanisms and generalized median schemes, quasi-compensatory incentive schemes and contracts under observable actions), and priorities are delineated by uniform rules; the areas where the two traditions diverge are identified, as are the dimensions of the problem (staff, structure, institutions, awareness, agents' beliefs) covered only by TCO.

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) now assist users across sessions of images and text, carried by an external memory of what was said and shown. When such an assistant answers wrongly, the failure usually began earlier, in how a record was written, updated or retrieved, and the answer alone does not say where. We formalize multimodal memory as four stages, Write, Update, Retrieve and Answer, and define nine error types across them. A stage-resolved analysis on Mem-Gallery traces most failures to a source stage, and most of those lie before the answer. Injecting known errors against fact-preserving control edits, we then follow each tainted record downstream. Early errors survive to the answer as apparent evidence, and hurt most when no other record holds the fact. A diagnosis that trusts the quoted evidence therefore blames the stage where the error surfaces, not the one where it began. We propose MemDoctor, in which the MLLM that built the memory diagnoses its own failures. It traces each needed fact backward through the four stages, accepts a diagnosis only when the cited evidence is found in memory, and repairs that stage before answering again. On a 4B backbone, MemDoctor improves accuracy on both Mem-Gallery and MemLens, outperforming all evaluated 8B baselines, and the same loop also improves MuRAG and A-Mem.
